lessons.title: What LGAR-C actually models
lessons.summary: Separate soil infiltration, catchment runoff, and river hydraulics.

A catchment is an area whose water can reach a common outlet. Rain arriving there can remain on the surface, enter soil, return to the air, or leave toward a stream. A rainfall–runoff model estimates those amounts through time. A hydrodynamic model instead solves water motion and water levels in channels or across terrain. These are different jobs. A runoff depth alone cannot tell you which building floods.

LGAR means Layered Green and Ampt with Redistribution. It represents water moving through a vertical stack of soil layers. Redistribution means water continues moving after rain stops. The repository name remains LGAR-C, but its README calls the complete catchment model CASAM: Catchment Arid/Semi-arid Model. LASAM is an earlier name still present in executable and library names. The suffix C does not establish the language standard: the active implementation uses C++14 and a small C routing function.

content.caption: Components and their jobs

rows.text: A list of boundaries between wetter and drier soil regions
Coordinates rainfall, soil, evaporation, delayed stores, and output
One or two abstract water stores with storage-dependent discharge
A queue spreads a runoff pulse over later intervals

inline.text: The vadose zone is soil above the water table where pore spaces need not be full of water. Infiltration is entry through its top. Percolation is downward movement inside or out of it. Surface runoff is water that remains available to leave over land. Interflow is a modeled lateral loss from soil toward the outlet. Baseflow is delayed stream supply often associated with groundwater; a conceptual reservoir can imitate some of its timing without solving an actual groundwater pressure field.

The model was designed around precipitation partitioning in arid and semi-arid settings. That is a process emphasis, not a guarantee based on a climate label. Dry places can contain irrigated fields, shallow groundwater, fractured rock, or urban drainage that violate the simple column representation. Conversely, a well-drained soil experiment in a wetter region can still be a useful test of infiltration mechanics.

content.title: Follow a storm without double counting
content.scenario: A hypothetical 10 mm storm produces 6 mm entry into soil, 3 mm surface runoff, and 1 mm bypass into a delayed store. There is no evaporation or initial ponding.

steps.text: Account for the input once: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 mm.
Treat bypass as an internal transfer into the delayed store, not immediate outlet flow.
Retain runoff still waiting in the outlet queue when checking the catchment balance.

content.result: The partition closes, but the outlet may discharge less than 4 mm during the storm.
content.interpretation: Delayed storage changes timing. It does not create additional rainfall.

inline.text: A coastal surge, backwater from a river, sewer surcharge, or floodplain water-level map requires information and equations this soil-column model does not provide. Use CASAM as a runoff source only where the receiving model and coupling are suitable.

content.title: Good runoff volume, wrong flood extent
content.observed_behavior: Total simulated runoff matches an event estimate, but a proposed flood map is wrong.
content.conditions: Only catchment runoff depths were modeled.
content.candidate_causes: Terrain error; missing water-level and flow equations; a soil parameter error.
content.reasoning: The immediate problem is a missing spatial hydraulics model. Tuning soil conductivity cannot invent channel geometry or downstream water levels.
content.recommended_action: Separate runoff validation from inundation modeling, then identify the required receiving model and boundary data.

lessons.title: Depth, rates, and conservation
lessons.summary: Build water accounting from units before reading the model loops.

inline.text: Largest accepted absolute substep water-balance error before abort.
An accounting equation comparing water present initially, water entering, water leaving, and water remaining.

Imagine putting a bookkeeping boundary around a soil column. Water inside is storage. Water crossing the boundary is an input or output. This imagined boundary is a control volume. In catchment modeling we often divide water volume by ground area and report an equivalent water depth. One millimeter spread across one square meter is one liter. A depth is an amount per area; a depth per hour is a rate. Their variable types may both be double, but their meanings differ.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

content.accessible_text: Rain depth D equals intensity i times duration delta t.

inline.text: The multiplication follows by adding equal small portions of rain over time. If the rate changes, split the interval and sum each rate times its own duration. That sum becomes an integral as intervals become arbitrarily small. This is the practical meaning of integration used here; it is accumulation, not a mysterious new kind of water.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Water inside all selected stores at start
Water leaving an uncoupled lower boundary
Water in all selected stores at end
Unaccounted water; sign indicates excess or deficit

content.accessible_text: Residual epsilon equals initial storage plus precipitation minus evaporation, outlet flow, lower-boundary loss, and final storage.

inline.text: Choose the boundary before using the equation. For a soil-only balance, infiltration is input and interflow is output. For the full catchment, transfer from soil to a reservoir stays inside the boundary and cancels between the two ledgers. Include surface ponding, both reservoirs, and runoff waiting in the routing queue if those stores fall inside your boundary. Do not subtract both raw runoff and its routed discharge as separate external losses.

content.title: A five-minute substep
content.scenario: Rain intensity is 12 mm/h for a 300-second model substep.

steps.text: Convert time: 300/3600 = 1/12 h.
Multiply intensity by duration: 12 × 1/12 = 1 mm.
Convert depth: 1 mm = 0.1 cm = 0.001 m.

content.result: The substep receives 0.1 cm, not 1.2 cm.
content.interpretation: `Update` converts millimeters to centimeters and multiplies by `subtimestep_h`.

content.title: A complete ledger
content.scenario: Start storage is 20 cm; rain is 1 cm; actual evaporation is 0.1 cm; outlet discharge is 0.2 cm; uncoupled lower loss is 0.05 cm.

steps.text: Expected final storage is 20 + 1 − 0.1 − 0.2 − 0.05 = 20.65 cm.
If recorded final storage is 20.60 cm, compute residual 0.05 cm.

content.result: 0.05 cm is unaccounted for.
content.interpretation: It may be a missed store or a numerical defect. The sign alone does not locate the error.

inline.text: Conservation is necessary but insufficient. A program sending all rainfall directly to the outlet can conserve water perfectly while representing soil behavior poorly. The configured mass-balance tolerance is an abort threshold in centimeters, not a prediction-accuracy target. Increasing it prevents some stops while permitting a larger accounting defect.

content.title: Runoff is exactly ten times too large
content.observed_behavior: A model chain produces a clean factor-of-ten difference.
content.conditions: One interface uses centimeters and another uses millimeters.
content.reasoning: An exact scale factor suggests an interface conversion first. It does not prove the cause; compare the earliest point of divergence.
content.recommended_action: Log input rate, duration, converted depth, and output units at one interval. Then close the ledger independently.

lessons.title: Water content, pressure, and change
lessons.summary: Introduce the mathematical and physical quantities used by the soil functions.

inline.text: Approach toward a limiting answer as numerical resolution or iteration accuracy improves.
The local rate at which one quantity changes as another changes.
Change in a quantity divided by the distance over which it changes.
Water volume divided by total soil volume; 0.25 means one quarter of the sample volume is water.
The pull retaining water in soil pores, expressed here as a positive equivalent water-column height.

Soil contains solid material and spaces between grains. Water content is the fraction of total soil volume occupied by water. A value of 0.25 means a one-liter soil sample contains 0.25 liters of water. It is not a water depth and is not the fraction of pores filled. The latter requires knowing how much pore space exists. In this code, theta_e is the upper water-content value and theta_r is a fitted residual value at the dry end of the curve.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Water volume divided by bulk soil volume
Equivalent water depth in the layer
Position within the residual-to-upper water range

rows.constraints: greater than theta_r and less than 1

content.accessible_text: Stored water depth is water content times layer thickness. Effective saturation is water content above residual divided by the available water-content range.

inline.text: Water clings to grains and small openings. Removing it from a drier soil requires stronger suction. A pressure head expresses pressure as the height of an equivalent water column. Many texts use a negative pressure head for unsaturated soil. LGAR generally stores the positive magnitude as psi_cm: larger means drier. It is not elevation and not ponded water depth. Equal pressure head in different soil types need not mean equal water content.

A derivative describes a local rate of change: front velocity is depth change divided by a very small time change. A finite step replaces that small change with a chosen interval. A gradient is the same idea across distance: a difference in head divided by separation. A partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. We need these ideas to describe water that changes with both depth and time; no prior calculus is assumed.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

content.accessible_text: Next front depth is approximately current depth plus current velocity times the time step.

inline.text: This update treats velocity as constant over a step. That approximation becomes risky near a soil boundary or when a thin wet region changes quickly. Stability concerns whether perturbations and errors propagate in a controlled way over the interval being solved. Bounded output is only one diagnostic. A consistent approximation approaches the intended equation as steps shrink; convergence means a sequence of refined results approaches a limit. These are separate tests. A cap can keep a variable bounded while making its value inaccurate.

content.title: Same soil, three meanings
content.scenario: A 40 cm layer has theta = 0.30, theta_r = 0.10, and theta_e = 0.50.

steps.text: Water depth is 0.30 × 40 = 12 cm.
Effective saturation is (0.30 − 0.10)/(0.50 − 0.10) = 0.50.
A 0.02 increase in water content adds 0.8 cm of water if thickness stays fixed.

content.result: The soil contains 12 cm water and has effective saturation 0.5.
content.interpretation: Neither quantity is a pressure head. Do not pass one where the other is expected.

content.title: Wrong response to drying
content.observed_behavior: A coupling sends increasingly negative head values and fractional powers fail.
content.conditions: The receiving soil function expects positive suction magnitude.
content.candidate_causes: Invalid sign convention; a dry-soil limit; a memory error.
content.reasoning: Negative inputs to a noninteger power may produce a non-number even when the physical state is meaningful under a different sign convention.
content.recommended_action: Check the declared head convention and convert at the boundary. Do not take absolute values indiscriminately for quantities that include positive ponded pressure.

lessons.title: From soil parameters to water and conductivity
lessons.summary: Derive and inspect the retention and conductivity functions.

inline.text: A relationship connecting suction strength with the fraction of soil volume occupied by water.
A fitted family of curves relating suction to moisture and, with a conductivity relation, soil water movement.

A retention curve connects suction to how much water remains in soil. It is an empirical relation: a compact equation fitted to observations rather than a complete description of every grain. The van Genuchten family supplies the retention relation used here. A second relation, commonly called van Genuchten–Mualem, estimates conductivity from effective saturation. Conductivity describes how readily water flows under a head gradient. Saturated conductivity Ks is the wet-end value; unsaturated conductivity K can be far smaller.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

content.accessible_text: m is one minus one over n. Effective saturation decreases with positive suction. Water content scales effective saturation between residual and upper content.

inline.text: The product alpha times psi must be dimensionless. Increasing alpha at the same positive suction reduces effective saturation; it shifts the drying curve to lower suction. The effect of n depends on where you are on the curve, so “larger n always means wetter” is not defensible. Setting n equal to one makes m zero and breaks inverse powers used elsewhere. A table of individually legal parameters can still describe an implausible soil if their combination is inconsistent.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

content.accessible_text: Invert the retention relation for suction; compute conductivity as saturated conductivity times a saturation-dependent factor.

inline.text: To obtain the inverse, raise effective saturation to minus one over m, subtract one, take the nth root, then divide by alpha. This is simply undoing the forward operations in reverse order. At saturation, suction tends to zero and conductivity tends to Ks. At the residual limit, suction tends toward infinity and conductivity toward zero. The code caps very large inverse heads at 10^20 cm; this is a numerical safeguard, not evidence that the physical soil has that measured suction.

content.title: Halfway through available water
content.scenario: Use theta_r = 0.10, theta_e = 0.50, theta = 0.30, alpha = 0.01 per cm, n = 2, and Ks = 1 cm/h.

steps.text: Effective saturation is 0.5 and m is 0.5.
Suction is 100 × sqrt(4 − 1) = 173.205 cm.
Conductivity is sqrt(0.5) × [1 − sqrt(0.75)] squared = approximately 0.012692 cm/h.

content.result: At effective saturation 0.5, conductivity is only about 1.27% of Ks.
content.interpretation: A linear conductivity guess of 0.5 Ks would badly overestimate flow for this parameter set.

inline.text: A single fitted retention curve does not explicitly track different wetting and drying paths, changing pore geometry, or multiple interacting pore systems. Parameter calibration may fit one record while failing under a different history.

content.title: Tiny n offset, huge trouble
content.observed_behavior: Dry parameter trials stall or produce zero conductivity.
content.conditions: n is only slightly greater than one.
content.candidate_causes: Ill-conditioned curve evaluation; invalid units; code ownership error.
content.reasoning: Small m produces extreme exponents and cancellation. Source comments identify near-one n as a difficult numerical regime.
content.recommended_action: Evaluate curves across the actual suction range before running events; distinguish an allowed parameter from a reliable calibration range.

lessons.title: Derive infiltration from a moving wetting front
lessons.summary: Use a simple front to understand the later layered algorithm.

inline.text: A stored boundary or layer-ending state used to represent differences in soil water content through depth.
A sharp moving boundary approximates the difference between wetter soil above and drier soil below.

A wetting front is a boundary between a wetter region and a drier region below it. The classical Green–Ampt picture replaces a smooth moisture profile with two uniform regions and a sharp boundary. It assumes a single homogeneous soil, a fixed moisture jump, and a saturated region above the front during ponded infiltration. This is a teaching limit, not the whole current LGAR implementation.

Darcy-style flow is conductivity times the driving head difference divided by the travel distance. With depth measured downward, gravity contributes a head difference equal to the front depth. Surface ponding and suction at the front add to that drive. Dividing their total by travel depth gives a dimensionless gradient. Multiplying by saturated conductivity gives an infiltration capacity.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Maximum intake rate in this idealized ponded case

content.accessible_text: Capacity equals saturated conductivity times gravity plus capillary and ponding drive over depth. Cumulative infiltration is moisture jump times front depth. Front speed is actual infiltration divided by the jump.

inline.text: Conservation gives the speed relation: moving the front one centimeter wets one centimeter of soil by the moisture jump. If that jump is 0.2, the move needs 0.2 cm of water. Delivering 0.1 cm in an hour advances it 0.5 cm. For constant ponded conditions the capacity can also be written as Ks times one plus capillary drive times moisture jump divided by cumulative infiltration. Integrating that relation yields an implicit time–infiltration relation; an explicit solver must still respect supply and surface storage.

content.title: A capacity calculation
content.scenario: Ks = 0.5 cm/h; suction = 10 cm; ponding = 0; front depth = 5 cm; moisture jump = 0.2.

steps.text: Gradient factor is 1 + 10/5 = 3.
Capacity is 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 cm/h.
With rainfall 1 cm/h and no stored ponding, actual infiltration is 1 cm/h.
With sufficient ponding, front speed would be 1.5/0.2 = 7.5 cm/h.

content.result: Capacity exceeds the first rain rate, so that rain can all infiltrate.
content.interpretation: Capacity is not a command to infiltrate water that does not exist.

inline.text: At large front depth the capillary contribution shrinks and this idealized capacity tends toward Ks. At depth approaching zero the expression becomes singular. An implementation must create a finite initial front or use an integrated start treatment. Do not “fix” the singularity by silently granting infinite water supply.

A uniformly wetted, deep, well-drained column is a good teaching case. Layer interfaces and interrupted rainfall stress the classical single-front assumptions. A rising shallow water table or lateral pressure-driven flow is outside this derivation. Averaging an intense short rainfall pulse into a gentle long pulse can reduce predicted infiltration-excess runoff because the averaged intensity may never exceed capacity.

content.title: No runoff after averaging rain
content.observed_behavior: Daily rainfall totals match, but computed storm peaks disappear.
content.conditions: Subhourly bursts were replaced with an hourly mean near the intake capacity.
content.candidate_causes: Routing lag; lost intensity information; incorrect soil depth.
content.reasoning: Infiltration depends nonlinearly on intensity. Smaller internal steps cannot recover a burst erased from the forcing.
content.recommended_action: Compare the original intensity series and event totals; test finer forcing before changing conductivity.

lessons.title: Why layers and redistribution change the problem
lessons.summary: Compare a moving-front approximation with a distributed flow equation.

inline.text: A depth- and time-dependent conservation equation that links water movement to pressure and moisture-dependent conductivity.

Consider a thin slab of soil. More water arriving through its top than leaving its bottom makes it wetter. Divide that difference by slab thickness and let the slab become very thin: local storage change is minus the depth derivative of downward flow. Add a local removal term for roots or evaporation. This is conservation at every depth rather than only for one whole column.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Water content at depth and time

rows.constraints: can be negative for upward flow

rows.meaning: Local water removal per bulk volume per time
Pressure head, negative in unsaturated soil

content.latex: \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial q}{\partial z}-s,\qquad q=K(\theta)\left(1-\frac{\partial h}{\partial z}\right)
content.accessible_text: With downward depth z and signed pressure head h, water-content change equals negative flow divergence minus removal; downward flow equals conductivity times gravity minus the signed-head gradient.

inline.text: Combining these relations with a retention curve produces a Richards-type equation. The word nonlinear matters: conductivity and water storage response change with the unknown moisture or head. A numerical solver divides depth and time into cells and intervals, estimates gradients, and often repeatedly solves for a self-consistent new state. Difficult dry fronts, strong soil contrasts, and boundary changes can demand smaller steps or more iterations. This explains a cost and robustness tradeoff; it does not mean every Richards solver is unreliable.

LGAR instead stores a small set of moving fronts and their water contents. It can represent more than one front and more than one soil layer. This retains event history more economically than a fixed fine grid in many cases, but it cannot reproduce every smooth moisture profile or every physical process supported by a suitable distributed solver. Agreement in total infiltration is weaker evidence than agreement in the entire moisture profile, drainage, and transient pressure.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Resistance for a common flux through layers

content.accessible_text: Series hydraulic resistance is the sum of thickness divided by conductivity; equivalent conductivity is total thickness divided by total resistance.

content.title: A thin barrier controls flow
content.scenario: Two equally thick 10 cm layers have conductivities 1 and 0.01 cm/h.

steps.text: Resistance is 10/1 + 10/0.01 = 1010 h.
Equivalent conductivity is 20/1010 = 0.019802 cm/h.
The arithmetic mean is 0.505 cm/h, over 25 times larger.

content.result: The low-conductivity layer dominates series resistance.
content.interpretation: The layered velocity implementation contains thickness/conductivity sums. This simple example explains their role, but is not its complete velocity equation.

inline.text: At a shared pressure head, layers with different retention parameters have different water contents. Copying theta across a boundary is therefore generally wrong. The source recomputes moisture and conductivity using each layer’s properties. During redistribution, conservation must also handle moving fronts that meet, cross a boundary, or leave the domain.

content.title: A comparison must hold boundaries fixed

inline.text: Compare LGAR with a Richards reference using the same initial head, soil curves, rainfall, surface condition, and lower boundary. Otherwise a difference cannot be assigned to the numerical method. A reference solver is not ground truth merely because it solves a more detailed equation.

content.title: Same total, different wetting profile
content.observed_behavior: Two models agree on runoff volume but disagree on moisture at 30 cm.
content.conditions: One represents sharp fronts and one uses a fine depth grid.
content.candidate_causes: Representation difference; sensor support volume; forcing mismatch.
content.reasoning: A local sensor and a front-region average are different observables. Volume agreement does not settle profile accuracy.
content.recommended_action: Compare depth-integrated water and sensor-scale averages, then refine the reference grid and examine front representation error.

inline.text: The inspected layered velocity adds a series-flow term and a capillary term, then divides by the moisture jump. For layers above the current front, the code evaluates moisture and conductivity at that front’s suction using each layer’s retention curve. This is more specific than simply replacing Ks by a harmonic mean everywhere.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Sum of traversed segment thickness over conductivity
Saturated conductivity in front layer after frozen reduction

content.accessible_text: Layered front velocity equals series-flow plus capillary-flow contributions divided by moisture jump.

inline.text: This expression is transcribed as mathematics from lgar_dzdt_calc, before velocity safeguards. Its gravity term has units centimeters divided by hours. Its capillary term has the same units. Dividing by a dimensionless moisture jump gives centimeters per hour. The upper-layer branch uses current unsaturated conductivity for the gravity contribution and a saturated-conductivity capillary term. Do not label every LGAR front as saturated.

The reviewed LGAR paper assumes uniform hydraulic properties within each layer, one capillary head across a layer interface, no material influence from a near-surface water table, isothermal solute-free water, and no flowing gas phase. Its multi-month comparisons support arid and semi-arid use where cumulative potential evapotranspiration exceeds cumulative precipitation; they do not establish unrestricted wet-climate or groundwater-coupled validity.

lessons.title: Representing and conserving a front list
lessons.summary: Connect physical regions to pointer ownership and topology changes.

inline.text: A comparison that detects changes from a recorded expected behavior; preserving behavior alone does not prove scientific correctness.

A linked list stores records connected by pointers. LGAR uses each wetting-front record to describe a moisture boundary or layer-ending state. The head pointer identifies the first record. The next pointer links to another record. The fields include front depth, water content, suction, conductivity, layer number, and a flag named to_bottom. A soil layer is a fixed material region; a wetting front is a changing moisture feature. Their counts need not match.

The flag to_bottom marks a front record extending to the bottom of its material layer. In the velocity routine these layer-bottom records are stationary boundaries, unlike mobile interior fronts. Consecutive layer-bottom records can form a stack sharing suction. They still have different moisture values because each layer has its own retention curve. Deleting a layer-bottom record as if it were a redundant interior front can destroy the representation.

Many soil arrays are one-indexed, with index zero reserved for a boundary or unused entry. Most C++ callers expect zero-indexed arrays. The driver explicitly translates some arrays, including routing ordinates. Never infer indexing from the language. Inspect allocation length, initialization loop, and export pointer together. Reading n values from an n+1 allocation may stay inside memory while still returning the wrong n values.

Storage is a sum of water content times represented thickness. Regions must be counted exactly once. A front depth measured from the surface is not automatically a region thickness; subtract the appropriate preceding boundary.
lgar_calc_mass_bal

traverses this representation. The time integrator saves a previous-state copy because the current list is changed during a substep. Replacing that copy with an alias would erase the old state needed by later calculations.

content.title: A conservative merge
content.scenario: Two adjacent regions in the same material are 4 cm thick at water content 0.40 and 6 cm thick at 0.20.

steps.text: Their water depth is 4 × 0.40 + 6 × 0.20 = 2.8 cm.
A single 10 cm region preserving water would have content 2.8/10 = 0.28.
An unweighted average gives 0.30 and stores 3.0 cm.

content.result: The unweighted merge creates 0.2 cm of water.
content.interpretation: This is a pedagogical conservation example, not a replacement for the repository’s full front-merge algorithm or equal-head constraints.

content.caption: Pinned correction dispatcher after front movement

rows.text: A wetter front overtakes a deeper same-layer front
Use thickness-weighted mass, not a plain moisture average
A front passes a layer-bottom record
Cross the layer boundary and restore equal head
Recompute layer-specific moisture and correct residual mass
A front passes the model bottom
Do not silently delete the overshoot
A shallower same-layer region is drier than the region below
Adjust head/moisture iteratively and return mass change to the ledger

inline.text: The dispatcher runs until it returns zero. A merge can expose a layer crossing, and a crossing can create a dry-over-wet state. The order is therefore part of the numerical method. Termination, mass residual, equal-head continuity, front ordering, and stable identifiers should all be asserted in transition tests.

A front meeting another front, reaching a layer bottom, or leaving the domain changes the list topology: which records exist and how they connect. The source has dedicated merge, layer-crossing, domain-crossing, and dry-over-wet correction routines. A generic list cleanup can therefore change physics. Check storage immediately before and after a topology operation, allowing only explicitly recorded boundary transfers.

The BMI adapter exports flat arrays for front depths and water contents. It deletes and reallocates those arrays during updates. A pointer acquired before an update must not be assumed valid afterward. Reacquire both the grid size and pointer after the update, or use copying access into a caller-owned buffer. Even a pointer that happens to keep the same address does not establish a lifetime guarantee.

content.title: Parallel execution is an ownership question

inline.text: There is no demonstrated within-column parallel solver here. Running independent columns in separate processes is a possible orchestration strategy, not a claim of thread safety. Global variables, shared output files, and model instance state need review before concurrent use.

content.title: A crash appears only after heavy rain
content.observed_behavior: An external wrapper holds a front-moisture pointer between model updates.
content.conditions: Heavy rain changes front count; export arrays are reallocated.
content.candidate_causes: Stale pointer; new physical instability; bad compiler.
content.reasoning: The rainfall connection can be indirect: a state change triggers reallocation, then the caller reads freed storage.
content.recommended_action: Use an address sanitizer in a development build and reacquire the exported buffer after every update. Preserve the rainfall case as a regression test.

Estimating accumulated area under a curve using a finite set of evaluations, such as trapezoids.
Approximate area under a curve by average endpoint height times interval width.
Conductivity varies through the transition from wetter to drier soil. The effective capillary drive summarizes part of this behavior as a length. In the numerical path,
calc_Geff

converts the two moisture limits to suction limits, integrates conductivity with respect to suction, and divides by saturated conductivity. The wet side has smaller suction and the dry side larger suction. The final absolute value enforces the positive convention, but it should not replace checking whether the supplied moisture ordering is physically valid.

content.accessible_text: Effective capillary drive is the conductivity integral over suction divided by saturated conductivity. A trapezoid estimates each piece using average endpoint conductivity times head width.

inline.text: The trapezoid rule approximates a curve by a straight segment between two sampled values. In source,
nint

seeds the first trial width; it is not the final number of equal intervals. The trial shrinks if endpoint conductivity changes by more than roughly two percent relative to the later value. Accepted steps increase the next trial width by a factor of ten. The accepted area uses the actual width after clipping to the upper bound, which matters for the final trapezoid.

content.title: Dimensional check on an integral
content.scenario: For a simplified constant conductivity of 0.2 cm/h over a 10 cm suction interval, use Ks = 1 cm/h.

steps.text: Integral area is 0.2 × 10 = 2 cm squared per hour.
Divide by 1 cm/h to obtain 2 cm.

content.result: G is 2 cm.
content.interpretation: It is a head-like length, not an infiltration rate. It must be combined with conductivity and geometry to affect velocity.

inline.text: A two-percent endpoint-change check is not a rigorous bound on total integral error. The routine uses a minimum step and a maximum iteration count. If the iteration cap stops integration early, the visible function does not return an explicit failure flag. The h_min conditional has no active correction. These are observed control-flow facts; whether they harm a particular input requires a targeted experiment.

The other path uses a Brooks–Corey-based closed-form approximation and substitutes its capillary scale when the result is infinite or not a number. It is not simply an exact, faster evaluation of the numerical van Genuchten integral. Compare the numerical path against independently refined quadrature first, then compare the closed-form path against that result. Otherwise discretization error and formulation difference are mixed together.

Well-ordered limits within a validated soil curve are a suitable test. Extremely dry conditions, n near one, and nearly coincident moisture bounds stress arithmetic. A negative Ks or invalid retention range is an invalid input, not an invitation to accept whatever finite fallback appears.

content.reasoning: The switch changes mathematical formulation. Matching a finite value is not proof of equivalence.
content.recommended_action: Record G for representative states, compare numerical refinement, and trace the changed intake capacity into the surface-water budget.

inline.text: The closed-form branch uses a positive Brooks–Corey pore-distribution parameter lambda and a positive capillary scale psi_b. Here lambda controls the powers applied to effective saturation; psi_b has units of centimeters and sets the driving-head scale. Both arise from the soil parameter conversion in initialization, not from an independent observed water-level boundary.

The Basic Model Interface, abbreviated BMI, gives a caller common operations for initialization, update, access, and finalization. In this repository the main update advances through smaller soil substeps inside a forcing interval. Initialization reads configuration and constructs state. A caller supplies current rain and potential evaporation. Update converts units, selects a substep, copies old state, computes demands and movements, handles front topology, routes water, and exports outputs.
Read
BmiLGAR::Update

as an accounting transaction. Surface water begins with rain plus retained ponding. Optional bypass moves some to conceptual storage. Soil demand calculations are constrained by available water. Front creation or movement changes the soil representation. Merges and boundary crossings repair its topology. Interflow and lower losses must be included once in storage changes. Finally, interval totals are converted to interface units. A correct formula in the wrong position can double-count or delay a transfer.

Adaptive timestep here means a heuristic based on precipitation and ponding. It is not an embedded numerical method that estimates local truncation error and adjusts to an error tolerance. The chosen substep is capped by the forcing interval. The count of subcycles is computed by converting the interval/substep ratio to an integer after adding a small floating-point allowance. A noninteger ratio deserves explicit testing: the allowance corrects small representation errors near integers, not an arbitrary leftover fraction.

content.scenario: A fixed forcing interval is 3600 seconds and a fixed substep is 700 seconds.

steps.text: The ratio is about 5.142857.
Integer truncation gives five subcycles.
Five 700-second advances total 3500 seconds, leaving 100 seconds.

content.result: The simple subcycle arithmetic does not cover a full hour.
content.interpretation: This is a source-derived test hypothesis. Record actual time and rainfall depth to verify the complete execution path for this configuration.

inline.text: The front-velocity routine has lower and upper safeguards. It can substitute a very small positive velocity for a computed zero and cap a very large velocity. Such safeguards can prevent pathological states or preserve special control semantics, but they alter the numerical evolution. A run that finishes is not necessarily converged. Compare results across decreasing valid substeps, while holding forcing samples and all physical parameters fixed.

lessons.summary: Trace atmospheric demand, actual removal, and drainage options.

inline.text: Positive suction magnitude used as the dry end of actual-evapotranspiration reduction.
Positive suction magnitude used as the wetter reference for evaporation reduction.
Uses bottom conductivity to remove water through the lower boundary.
Subtracts potential evapotranspiration from precipitation before partitioning when enabled.

Evapotranspiration combines evaporation to the air and transpiration through plants. Potential evapotranspiration, PET, is atmospheric demand under a reference supply assumption. Actual evapotranspiration, AET, is water the model can actually remove. They are not interchangeable forcing fields. The code reduces demand using the surface front’s suction and then applies water-availability checks elsewhere in Update.

Field capacity is an operational wetness reference associated with slowed drainage; it is not a universal exact soil constant. The wilting-point reference represents very difficult water extraction. The code converts both configured suction heads to moisture, averages those two moisture values, then converts that average back to suction. This produces the half-demand head used by the reduction curve. Averaging the two heads directly gives a different result because retention is nonlinear.

The displayed smooth demand equation applies only within the source’s active branch: surface suction must be below 1,000,000 cm. At or above that threshold, calc_aet returns zero demand. The guard is a numerical dry-state protection; it is not a universal physiological wilting law. Additional storage limits can reduce the requested amount further.

content.scenario: PET is 0.2 cm/h, duration is 0.5 h, and surface suction equals the half-demand head.

Denominator is 1 + 1 cubed = 2.
Requested removal is 0.05 cm.

content.interpretation: Cubing the entire expression (1 + ratio) instead would give one eighth demand. The file header’s notation is ambiguous; executable operations settle the difference.

inline.text: A no-flow lower boundary sets no continuous drainage through the column base. A free-drainage choice removes water according to bottom conductivity, subject to storage and dry-state guards. The option to send drainage to conceptual reservoirs changes the destination: it remains inside catchment storage instead of leaving as uncoupled recharge. This is separate from explicit handling of fronts reaching or crossing the modeled domain.

With a genuinely deep, dry profile, surface-driven losses may dominate and lower-boundary choice may have little effect for a short experiment. With a wet shallow profile, the choice can strongly affect storage and delayed runoff. Neither option imposes an observed, time-varying groundwater head. A rising water table can generate upward supply that this free-drainage formulation does not represent.
calc_aet

receives a rate despite its PET argument name lacking a per-hour suffix. It multiplies by duration internally. The AET threshold and exponent arguments are reported as unused in the current calculation. Do not expect calibration of an unused argument to change the result.

lessons.summary: Explain thresholded recharge, two stores, and explicit discharge.

A conceptual reservoir is an abstract store described by a water amount and a release rule. It need not correspond to a literal underground tank. Preferential flow means water bypassing much of the soil matrix through more connected paths. CASAM imitates part of that behavior with a threshold and fractional allocation, not a resolved network of cracks or large pores. The top-front wetness and previous-step flags affect activation, so trace the update order rather than assuming instantaneous switching.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

content.accessible_text: Reservoir discharge rate is a times storage to power b. The explicit update adds input depth and subtracts discharge computed from old storage.

inline.text: Units follow from the required rate: multiplying a by storage raised to b must give centimeters per hour. Thus a has units centimeters raised to one minus b per hour. If b changes, comparing the bare numerical values of a becomes misleading. For b equal to one, the coefficient has units per hour and its reciprocal is a characteristic drainage time. For larger b, high storage releases water disproportionately quickly.

content.title: One explicit reservoir step
content.scenario: Old storage is 2 cm, input is 0.1 cm/h, a is 0.2 per hour, b is one, and the step is 0.5 h.

steps.text: Rate from old storage is 0.2 × 2 = 0.4 cm/h.
Release depth is 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 cm.
Recharge depth is 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 cm.
New storage is 2 + 0.05 − 0.2 = 1.85 cm.

content.result: Release is 0.2 cm and final storage is 1.85 cm.
content.interpretation: Do not return a rate where the function returns a substep depth.

inline.text: calc_CR_Q

partitions recharge between a fast and a slow store. The slow fraction receives its share of input and the fast store gets the remainder. Each store has its own coefficient and exponent. The function returns the sum of the two release depths. Its code sets release to zero below 0.01 cm initial storage and clips a release that would drive updated storage negative. That enforces nonnegative storage but does not establish temporal accuracy.

For a linear store with no input, exact exponential decay over a step is always positive. The explicit method multiplies storage by one minus a times duration. If that factor becomes negative, the unconstrained method fails; clipping empties the store in one step instead. A converged simulation requires a sufficiently small step or a different integration rule, not merely a nonnegative result.

One or two stores can approximate delayed recession shapes. A calibrated fast/slow split does not prove two real aquifers exist. Different input partitions, coefficients, and exponents may fit similar outlet records. A connected groundwater pressure field or pumping response requires a different physical representation.

content.candidate_causes: Overfitting; forcing bias; wrong boundary process.
content.reasoning: More flexibility can fit an error source without representing it. Better training fit alone is not evidence of correct groundwater physics.
content.recommended_action: Hold out contrasting events and compare water balance, recession timing, and independent storage observations.

lessons.summary: Separate a lateral-loss parameterization from the delay queue.

inline.text: Ordered nonnegative weights used by the unit-hydrograph convolution.

Interflow is water removed from soil toward a stream without traveling over the surface. In this implementation both interflow parameters must be specified to enable it. A front becomes eligible when its positive suction is at or below the threshold: smaller suction means wetter. The factor scales candidate removal through conductivity and the represented share of column depth. It folds unresolved geometry and connectivity into one coefficient; it does not solve a lateral head gradient.

Candidate removal is not necessarily actual removal. The algorithm limits extraction by removable storage. For a deepest stack of layer-bottom fronts sharing suction, it adjusts a common suction and recomputes each layer’s moisture, rather than independently subtracting arbitrary water from one front. A bisection solve repeatedly halves an interval bracketing the required suction until the resulting stack water approaches the target. Shared head preserves compatibility across materials whose moisture values differ.

content.interpretation: The remaining request is not real discharge unless water is actually removed and accounted for.

inline.text: A geomorphological instantaneous unit hydrograph, GIUH, is a delay distribution used here as discrete weights. In ordinary terms, it splits each arriving runoff pulse across present and later intervals. The current driver sends surface runoff, interflow, and conceptual-reservoir release into this routing calculation. The queue accumulates contributions from multiple past pulses. The name does not mean a resolved channel-flow solver.

Fraction released at a specified delay

content.scenario: An isolated 10 mm pulse enters an empty queue with weights 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3.

content.interpretation: A test ending after the first interval must include 8 mm queued storage.

inline.text: The BMI output labeled total discharge is a water depth in meters for an interval, not cubic meters per second. To obtain a volume rate, multiply by catchment area in square meters and divide by actual interval duration in seconds. One millimeter over two square kilometers in one hour is 2000 cubic meters divided by 3600 seconds, or about 0.556 cubic meters per second.

content.reasoning: Check actual removal and queued storage before declaring a mass leak. Delayed release is expected from convolution.

inline.text: The reduction routine compares soil-temperature coordinates directly with cumulative layer depths, while nearby documentation and BMI comments do not consistently state the same length unit. Also, the new-surface-front path passes an already reduced saturated conductivity into the unsaturated-conductivity function and multiplies its result by frozen_factor again. The source proves these operations exist; without a controlled run it does not prove their production impact. Test units and the expected single-versus-squared reduction before relying on coupled results.

These statements are source observations, not measured frequency or impact claims. A defect report should include the exact commit, minimal configuration, caller sequence, expected contract, observed result, and relevant source lines. Separate a reproducible failure from a hypothesis about production behavior. Some callers may never use a faulty method, while another may trigger it immediately.

Soil Freeze Thaw, SFT, supplies temperature-related information used to reduce hydraulic conductivity when soil is frozen. The example coupled workflow also uses a soil-moisture-profile component to relate front states to another model’s depth representation. Mapping fronts to fixed depths is a data transformation with its own averaging and unit choices. A nominally successful connection does not prove those spatial representations agree.

inline.text: A freeze/thaw reduction should generally reduce matrix infiltration capacity under otherwise comparable conditions, which can raise available surface runoff. lessons.summary: Build evidence beyond a successful executable and one benchmark.

inline.text: Allows qualifying dry-period fluxes to be reused between full calculations.
Checking that implementation matches intended equations and interface contracts.

Verification asks whether code implements its intended mathematics and contracts. Validation asks whether the model is adequate for the real situation and observations. Regression testing asks whether behavior changed from an earlier version. A preserved old answer can still be physically wrong. A realistic hydrograph can still hide a unit defect. Use all three kinds of evidence.

The repository includes a BMI unit-test driver and synthetic examples with comparison outputs. They provide useful starting cases, including precipitation pulses and interface checks. Inspect which assertions actually execute in the pinned tests. The README’s list is not a formal coverage guarantee. A one-interval benchmark cannot establish year-long conservation, restart fidelity, or behavior at every front transition.

content.caption: A focused test portfolio

rows.text: Input equals storage gain plus external losses
Incorrect region thickness or duplicate removal
Outputs approach a stable reference trend
Units, values, size, and time agree

inline.text: Performance depends on the number of active fronts, list traversals and copies, soil-function evaluations, quadrature retries, subcycles, and logging. It is not enough to report CPU utilization. Measure elapsed time, allocation counts where possible, active-front counts, and time spent in hot functions. Profile representative dry periods and storms separately because their control paths differ.

Flux caching reuses results under qualifying dry and slow conditions. The source can defer front movement and potential-evaporation corrections, with later reconciliation. Its reset threshold is counted in timesteps; treating that unconditionally as 24 wall-clock hours assumes the expected interval length. Interflow eligibility disables caching. Consequently a speedup measured with interflow off may not transfer to a wet, interflow-active catchment.

content.title: Interpret a caching experiment
content.scenario: An uncached run takes 100 seconds and a cached run takes 40 seconds. Both use identical inputs and a measured runoff-volume difference is 0.3%.

steps.text: Speedup is 100/40 = 2.5.
Also compare peak timing, cumulative balance, soil storage, and dry-period drainage.
Specify an application-dependent acceptable difference before choosing the faster path.

content.result: The speedup is 2.5, but volume agreement alone does not establish acceptability.
content.interpretation: A small annual difference can hide a large event or low-flow difference.

content.title: Change one cause at a time

inline.text: Enabling caching, adaptive stepping, a closed-form capillary approximation, and a new compiler at once makes a speedup hard to explain. Start from a reproducible baseline, isolate each change, then test interactions.

content.title: A test passes while a caller crashes
content.observed_behavior: Upstream BMI tests pass but another framework crashes when obtaining grid shape.
content.conditions: The callers allocate different buffer lengths or exercise different methods.
content.candidate_causes: Untested interface method; caller bug; size contract mismatch.
content.reasoning: A passing suite establishes only the cases it exercises. A rank-one shape written at index one can remain hidden by an oversized test buffer.
content.recommended_action: Add a minimal correctly sized guarded-buffer test and preserve the original passing test. Do not weaken the contract to fit the implementation.

lessons.title: Calibration, sensitivity, and identifiable claims
lessons.summary: Explain what a fitted parameter can and cannot tell you.

inline.text: Enables BMI access to selected calibration parameters.
Interprets only the documented conductivity, alpha, reservoir-a, and interflow values as base-ten logarithms.

Calibration selects parameters to improve agreement with observations. Sensitivity asks how an output changes when an input or parameter changes. Identifiability asks whether the available observations can distinguish competing parameter values. A parameter can strongly affect output and still be hard to identify if another parameter offsets its effect. A good fit is evidence about that experiment, not a certificate that the internal process is correct.

Separate error classes before tuning: precipitation may be biased; soil parameters may be wrong; initial storage may be wrong; a boundary may omit an important source; the timestep may be too coarse; floating-point evaluation may fail; an interface may mislabel units; or the model may omit the needed physical process. Parameter optimization can conceal several of these errors by compensation.

content.caption: Quantities used in the following equation

rows.meaning: Base-ten logarithm of numerical value in prescribed units

content.accessible_text: Mean squared error averages squared prediction errors. In a base-ten log parameterization, physical parameter x is ten raised to stored value u.

inline.text: Squared error weights large absolute errors heavily. It can prioritize high flows while underemphasizing relative low-flow errors. Evaluate event volume, peak timing, recession shape, and storage as distinct observables rather than relying on one objective. Align timestamps and compare the same spatial and temporal support: an instantaneous measurement differs from an interval mean.

content.title: Log mode changes the meaning of a number
content.scenario: A desired conductivity is 0.1 cm/h and log_mode is enabled.

steps.text: The base-ten logarithm of 0.1 is −1.
An input of 0.1 would instead represent 10 to the power 0.1, about 1.258925 cm/h.
The incorrect physical value is about 12.59 times the intended value.

content.result: Use −1 for this conductivity in the documented log-mode path.
content.interpretation: Log transforms apply to selected named parameters; do not transform every field indiscriminately.

inline.text: Use physically coherent ranges, not only every range that survived a stability test. Soil texture can make parameter combinations correlated. Vary one parameter first to learn its local effect, then explore interactions. Split calibration and evaluation periods by contrasting conditions when possible. Include dry-to-wet transitions, intense storms, and different initial storage, not random timestamps that leak nearly identical events into both sets.

content.title: When tuning cannot repair the model

inline.text: If runoff is caused by a water table rising from below, lowering saturated conductivity may mimic more runoff while producing a wrong moisture mechanism. Calibration cannot add upward groundwater boundary forcing or a resolved floodplain. State the missing process and consider another formulation.

content.title: Excellent flow fit, wrong moisture
content.observed_behavior: Outlet error is low but simulated soil stays too wet.
content.conditions: Evaporation and reservoir parameters were calibrated only to outlet flow.
content.candidate_causes: Parameter compensation; biased observations; missing drainage.
content.reasoning: The outlet alone may not identify internal partitioning. Water can reach the right outlet at the right time through a wrong path.
content.recommended_action: Add independent moisture or evaporation constraints, inspect total storage and drainage, and evaluate on withheld conditions.

lessons.title: Model selection from assumptions and evidence
lessons.summary: Make defensible choices under good, marginal, and inappropriate conditions.

inline.text: Disagreement caused by missing or unsuitable represented mechanisms, rather than only an incorrectly chosen parameter.

Model selection starts with the dominant process and the observable you need. “More physical” does not automatically mean better for a particular decision: a detailed model with poor boundary data can be less useful than a simpler model with well-constrained inputs. But simplicity does not excuse using a formulation that cannot represent the mechanism controlling the result.

content.caption: Choose a representation

rows.text: Simple derivation and event infiltration estimate
Single-front homogeneous assumptions in the teaching form
Layered columns and multiple wetting fronts with redistribution
Distributed head/moisture evolution with suitable boundaries
Nonlinear solves, discretization and boundary-data demands
Fitted stores do not establish groundwater geometry
Water levels and spatial flow when configured appropriately
Needs terrain, geometry, boundary and roughness information

inline.text: A good LGAR case is a well-characterized layered column where vertical matrix infiltration controls rainfall partitioning and the lower boundary is appropriate. Test against measurements or a converged reference using matching constitutive curves and boundary conditions. A marginal case is a profile with sharp contrasts, very dry states, or intense short storms sampled too coarsely. Here parameter uncertainty, capillary evaluation, and event timing deserve explicit sensitivity tests.

A clearly inappropriate standalone use is predicting inundation under coastal surge or strong river backwater. The missing quantity is not merely a better soil coefficient; it is the downstream water level and lateral flow dynamics. Similarly, interflow controlled by one multiplier does not resolve a mapped network of hillside groundwater heads. It can fit some responses without predicting how a new drainage intervention changes the pressure field.

content.caption: What the 2023 LGAR comparison does and does not establish

rows.text: Three arid or semi-arid USDA SCAN sites
Multi-month infiltration KGE 0.954-0.973 and NSE 0.971-0.995 against HYDRUS-1D
Strong agreement for the tested inputs and matched setup; not field truth or universal validity
Only about 0.3 cm cumulative difference, yet runoff KGE 0.688 and NSE 0.821
A small infiltration difference can be a large relative runoff error when nearly all rain infiltrates
PET set to zero in longer comparisons
Free-drainage results diverged as lower-profile heads evolved differently
Lower boundaries and climate regime are structural choices, not nuisance calibration details

content.title: Predict a conditional bias
content.scenario: Compare otherwise identical wet-soil runs. One mistakenly uses a saturated conductivity much larger than measured, and rainfall sometimes exceeds the true intake capacity.

steps.text: Larger conductivity tends to raise matrix intake capacity.
When water supply is sufficient and other limits do not dominate, more water enters soil.
This tends to reduce infiltration-excess surface runoff.

content.result: Expect underpredicted surface runoff in this specified regime.
content.interpretation: Do not claim the same sign for total delayed outlet flow under every reservoir and drainage configuration.

inline.text: Bias reasoning must name its conditions. Turning off a real groundwater contribution can underpredict delayed flow, but other calibrated pathways might compensate. Coarsening forcing can suppress intensity-driven peaks, but routing changes can modify their timing too. A useful hypothesis identifies which branch or equation changes and what competing effects could reverse the expected sign.

content.title: Where did the hydrograph go wrong?
content.observed_behavior: Peak volume is low, recession too slow, and soil storage high.
content.conditions: Rain total is credible; forcing is hourly; no-flow base and strong retention are configured.
content.candidate_causes: Smoothed intensity; too little drainage; routing too slow; conductivity compensation.
content.reasoning: Several mechanisms can coexist. Peak error points toward partitioning or timing; sustained storage error points toward losses or boundaries.
content.recommended_action: First verify units and balance. Then vary original forcing resolution, lower boundary, and routing separately. Compare intermediate fluxes, not only the final curve.

inline.text: For every comparison, predeclare what would falsify your hypothesis. If changing routing moves the peak without changing complete-event volume, that supports a timing explanation. If the total water differs after queues drain, inspect input, storage, losses, or weight normalization. Record rejected alternatives and uncertainty. An expert conclusion can be “these observations cannot distinguish the two mechanisms” when that is what the evidence supports.

lessons.title: A reproducible contribution and model audit
lessons.summary: Combine theory, source tracing, experiments, and a reviewable change.

inline.text: The ability to reconstruct a result from identified source, inputs, configuration, environment, and procedure.

The capstone has two tracks that meet in one reviewable evidence bundle. The software track audits the BMI layer-depth output. The modeling track examines an intense storm followed by a dry period in a layered column. Both require the same discipline: name the expected behavior, trace its source, test a discriminating case, and state what your evidence does not establish.

steps.text: Pin the source commit and create a separate working branch; preserve the unmodified baseline.
Initialize distinct layers, such as 10, 20, and 30 cm thickness, and derive cumulative bottoms 10, 30, and 60 cm.
Query advertised units and size, then copy the returned depth array into a correctly sized caller-owned buffer.
Compare against expected meters 0.1, 0.3, and 0.6; record the actual sentinel and unit behavior rather than assuming it.
Propose an adapter correction that preserves internal one-indexed centimeter arrays while exporting the promised representation.
Add a regression test for values, units, size, and pointer lifetime; test more than one layer count.

inline.text: A correction can translate at the adapter boundary or change internal representation. The first has a narrower effect but needs owned export storage and clear lifetime rules. The second reaches many soil routines and demands broader conservation testing. Explain this tradeoff rather than automatically rewriting the model. Avoid changing the public meaning silently; document compatibility for callers that may have compensated for the old behavior.

steps.text: Use a documented soil parameter set and explicit initial suction; record rainfall and evaporation units.
Run a baseline with caching disabled, divisible fixed substeps, explicit lower boundary, and recorded optional pathways.
Close soil and whole-catchment water balances with routing queue storage included.
Refine the internal step while keeping forcing unchanged, then separately examine finer original forcing if available.
Toggle one approximation or pathway at a time, including capillary calculation, caching, drainage, and interflow.
Compare infiltration, actual evaporation, soil storage, applied interflow, reservoir storage/release, and routed output.
Judge any reference-model comparison only after matching boundaries and validating the reference resolution.

content.title: A capstone interpretation
content.scenario: A routing change fixes peak timing while complete-event discharge remains unchanged. A lower-boundary change alters total discharge and final soil storage.

steps.text: The routing result supports a timing mechanism.
The boundary result changes the water ledger and delayed sources.
Neither result alone proves that a particular parameter set describes the real catchment.

content.result: Different symptoms identify different levels of the model chain.
content.interpretation: A single outlet objective would blur these explanations.

inline.text: Deliver the source revision, configuration and data checksums, command log, build environment, experiment table, unit ledger, plots with units, minimal failing test, proposed patch scope, and conclusion. Include whether model code was actually executed and which checks remain unrun. Do not paste predicted numbers into a results table as if measured.

The scored examination checks deterministic reasoning: numerical calculations, source-path selection, diagnosis, and model choice. The unscored implementation and experiment work provides practice and review evidence. Passing a generated quiz alone is not proof of independent research expertise or of the model’s suitability for a new basin.

content.title: A proposed fix improves everything at once
content.observed_behavior: A patch changes units, conductivity, routing weights, and timestep settings and reports a better hydrograph.
content.conditions: No isolated experiments or minimal tests are supplied.
content.reasoning: The comparison cannot establish which change fixed the defect, nor whether another change merely compensated for it.
content.recommended_action: Split changes, retain baseline results, require interface regression evidence for the adapter fix, and evaluate scientific changes in separate controlled experiments.
